findings.title: Azure YAML structural test parses only the header (splits off everything from `stages:`), so it cannot catch the production-deploy indentation bug (V017/V018)
findings.description: The sole structural-parse test for `azure_devops_yml` does `raw.split("\nstages:")[0] + "\nstages: []"` and only `yaml.safe_load`s the truncated header, discarding the ENTIRE stages body. The analogous GitLab test (`test_yaml_parses`, lines 862-866) parses the FULL document for every target via `yaml.safe_load(gitlab_ci_yml(target))`. The Azure equivalent was deliberately weakened to header-only, creating a coverage hole precisely over the broken region: the DeployProduction `env:` secrets block is under-indented (14 spaces under an 18-space `env:`), producing invalid YAML. Because the test throws the body away, CI is green while every emitted `.azure-pipelines.yml` is structurally invalid. This is the verified bug V017/V018.
findings.evidence: Executed (.venv python): header-only parse of azure_devops_yml('databricks') => OK (isinstance dict=True); full-document yaml.safe_load(azure_devops_yml('databricks')) => yaml.scanner.ScannerError: mapping values are not allowed here, line 194 '- script: |'. The weak test passes today; a full parse loop (what GitLab does) would fail for the targets, exposing the malformed DeployProduction env: block.
findings.recommended_fix: Replace the header-only test with a full-document parse loop mirroring the GitLab test: `for target in TARGETS: assert isinstance(yaml.safe_load(azure_devops_yml(target)), dict)`. This must be added/fixed ALONGSIDE the V017 source fix (depth-aware secrets indentation) — the test currently codifies a coverage hole and would otherwise keep the production bug invisible.

findings.title: No codegen test exercises a constant ENTRY with empty/missing name or None value, hiding the codegen<->executor divergence (V020) and the AttributeError crash (V021)
findings.description: The only constant-codegen tests cover an empty or None `values` LIST (the `{"constant": [0]}` default) and well-formed entries (`{"name": "rate", "value": "0.05"}`). They never test an individual entry with an empty/missing `name`, `name=None`, or `value=None`. Two verified bugs live exactly in that gap: (V021) `_gen_constant` calls `float(val)` then `_safe_str(val)` which does `None.replace(...)`, crashing for `value=None` even though the executor `_build_constant` tolerates it (`{name: [None]}`); (V020) for an empty/missing name `_gen_constant` emits a real column with default name (now `""`), while the executor `_build_constant` does `if not name: continue` and the column-contract `_constant_columns` keeps only truthy names — so a graph that runs in-canvas produces a different column set when saved/deployed. A user building a constant node with a blank row or a null value silently gets divergent generated code or a hard save/deploy crash, with no test guarding it.
findings.evidence: Executed (.venv python, _node_to_code): entry {name:'x', value:None} => raises AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'replace' (V021). entry {name:'', value:5} => codegen emits `return pl.LazyFrame({"": [5.0]})` AND decorator `contract={..."outputs": ['constant']}` — body column `""` vs executor/contract column `constant` (V020). src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:583-596 vs src/haute/_builders.py:604-628 confirm the divergence in source.
findings.recommended_fix: Add codegen tests (TDD, RED before the V020/V021 fix) asserting: (1) a constant node with an entry `{name:'x', value:None}` generates compilable code whose constant column equals the executor's (`[None]`), not a crash; (2) a constant node with an empty/missing-name entry produces the SAME column set the executor produces (entry skipped; `{"constant": [0]}` when all names empty) and a matching outputs contract. Cross-check generated `data_dict` against `_build_constant`'s runtime output for the same config.

findings.location: tests/test_rating_key_agreement.py:165-175 (test_string_keys_are_verbatim_never_collapsed) + :326-347 (test_legacy_compact_float_key_migrates_on_load); whole file lacks a string-label compact->expand round-trip
findings.title: No test pins compact->expand of a STRING factor label like "25.0"; the suite codifies the read-side migration as always-correct while the verified write/read asymmetry (V038) silently corrupts string labels
findings.description: The suite thoroughly covers numeric keys (`{"age": 25.0}` collapses to `"25"`) and the legacy read-side migration (`{"25.0": ...}` -> `"25"`), but never asserts that a row-array entry whose factor value is the STRING label `"25.0"` survives a fresh `compact_rating_step_config_for_sidecar` -> `expand_rating_step_config_from_sidecar` round trip. That is exactly the V038 bug: the write side (`_canonical_sidecar_key` -> `normalise_rating_key`) keeps string labels verbatim (`"25.0"`), so the compact map key is `"25.0"`; the read side (`_normalise_compact_sidecar_key`) then migrates `"25.0"` -> `"25"`. So a legitimate non-numeric band label `"25.0"` is silently rewritten after one save/load cycle. `test_legacy_compact_float_key_migrates_on_load` pins the migration as intended without distinguishing a true legacy float-key from a user's verbatim string label, effectively blessing the lossy behaviour. The matching read/write-collision case (V039: two labels differing only in float formatting written without a duplicate error but rejected on read) is also untested.
findings.evidence: Executed (.venv python): config entries=[{"age":"25.0","value":2.0}] => compact entries {'25.0': 2.0} => expand entries [{'age':'25','value':2.0}] ; LABEL PRESERVED? False. Source: src/haute/_rating_step_config.py:44-58 (write, verbatim) vs :61-79 (read, migrates int-like float-strings) and :225 walk() applying _normalise_compact_sidecar_key.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a RED test (alongside the V038/V039 fix) asserting a STRING factor label `"25.0"` round-trips compact->expand unchanged (or that the system fails loudly rather than silently collapsing it), and a test that two string labels differing only in float formatting (e.g. '5.' and '5') raise a duplicate on the WRITE side, symmetric with the read-side collision the suite already checks. Make the existing `test_legacy_compact_float_key_migrates_on_load` explicit that it targets legacy float keys, not user string labels.

findings.location: tests/test_fingerprint_cache.py:379-387 (TestGraphFingerprint.test_extra_keys_affect_fingerprint) — and the whole TestGraphFingerprint class
findings.title: graph_fingerprint tests never check injectivity of the extra_keys/context join; distinct cache contexts collide (V035) with no guarding test
findings.description: `TestGraphFingerprint` checks same-graph equality, different-node inequality, and that adding ONE extra key changes the fingerprint, but never probes the injectivity boundary the verified bug V035 concerns: `graph_fingerprint` joins `[*extra_keys, *context_parts, base]` with `"\n".join(...)`, which is NOT injective when an extra_key (or context part) contains a newline. Two semantically different cache contexts therefore produce an identical fingerprint, poisoning the cache (one request's result served for a structurally different one). No test in the suite (`test_fingerprint_cache.py`, `test_graph_fingerprint_cached.py`, `test_caching_correctness.py`) exercises a separator-bearing key.
findings.evidence: Executed (.venv python, haute._cache.graph_fingerprint): graph_fingerprint(g, 'a\nb') == graph_fingerprint(g, 'a', 'b') => both v5:7a01570ba0435ca9; COLLISION? True. (The node-id newline variant did NOT collide here, so the proven, scoped gap is the extra_keys/context join at src/haute/_cache.py:429-432.)
findings.recommended_fix: Add a test asserting `graph_fingerprint(g, 'a\nb') != graph_fingerprint(g, 'a', 'b')` (and a pipe/control-char variant), failing today, paired with the V035 fix that frames the join with canonical_json so each component is length-delimited and the encoding is injective.

findings.location: tests/test_caching_correctness.py (no _sort_key/NaN-set determinism test); tests/test_serialization_invariants.py (uses NaN values but not in sets)
findings.title: No test pins canonical_json order-independence for sets/frozensets containing NaN; the documented contract is silently violated (V034)
findings.description: canonical_json documents (module docstring + _canonicalise docstring) that unordered containers (set/frozenset) encode identically regardless of insertion order because they are sorted by `_sort_key`. That guarantee breaks when a set contains two or more NaN floats: `_sort_key` maps every float (NaN included) to ('2_num', value), and because all NaN comparisons are False, `sorted` cannot impose a total order and leaves the NaNs in hash/insertion order. Two logically-equal NaN-containing sets then canonicalise to different byte strings, so any cache key derived from such a value is non-deterministic. No test exercises a set/frozenset with NaN through canonical_json.
findings.evidence: Executed (.venv python, haute._cache.canonical_json): canonical_json(frozenset({nan,1.0,nan})) => '[NaN,1.0,NaN]' vs canonical_json(frozenset([1.0,nan,nan])) => '[1.0,NaN,NaN]'; stable across two equal NaN-sets? False. Source: src/haute/_cache.py _sort_key (~163-188) and the set branch (~137-147).
findings.recommended_fix: Add a determinism test asserting `canonical_json(set_a) == canonical_json(set_b)` for two equal NaN/inf-containing frozensets built in different orders (RED today), paired with the V034 fix that gives non-finite floats a stable, total secondary sort key.

findings.title: Cross-boundary submodel edge tests only cover single-submodel<->parent; the two-different-submodels child->child case (V041) is untested and the property suite explicitly budgets the bug out as accepted
findings.description: `TestMergeSubmodelsCrossBoundaryEdges` exercises reconstruction/rewiring of edges between ONE submodel's child and a main-file parent node (load->child_a, child_b->output), including dedup and membership guards. None of these reach the verified V041 case: a direct edge from an OUTPUT child of submodel A to an INPUT child of submodel B. There `rewire_edges` runs once per submodel; submodel A's pass rebuilds `submodel__A -> b_in` with sourceHandle='out__a_out', then submodel B's pass sees tgt_inside and clobbers it to `submodel__A -> submodel__B` WITHOUT preserving the sourceHandle — the boundary handle is lost (dropped on flatten, breaks codegen on re-save). The codegen roundtrip property test `test_submodel_container_types_are_explicitly_budgeted` documents this exact limitation ('drops user-facing cross-boundary source handles', 'a product limitation to fix') and pins NodeType.SUBMODEL out of the byte-idempotence property — i.e. the suite accepts the broken behaviour as known rather than asserting the correct (handle-preserving) outcome.
findings.evidence: Source: src/haute/_submodel_graph.py rewire_edges target-side branch does not pass sourceHandle (per VERIFIED-BUGS V041); tests/test_parser_submodels.py cross-boundary cases all use `{"sub": child}` (a single submodel). tests/test_codegen_roundtrip_property.py:707-717 docstring explicitly states the submodel parser 'drops user-facing cross-boundary source handles' and budgets it out.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a merge_submodels test with TWO submodels A and B and a parent_edges entry connecting a child of A directly to a child of B, asserting the rewired edge is `submodel__A -> submodel__B` with BOTH sourceHandle='out__a_out' AND targetHandle='in__b_in' preserved (and survives a flatten/codegen round trip). This is RED today and must land with the V041 fix; it also converts the property-test's 'known limitation' note into an enforced invariant.

findings.location: tests/test_codegen_docstring_roundtrip.py:36-40, 233-234, 559-569, 612-614 (module/class docstrings) vs the unmarked test bodies at :235-263, :559-614
findings.title: Docstring-roundtrip tests claim to be xfail(strict=True) / 'fails today' but carry no xfail marker and pass — misleading test documentation that obscures whether the invariant is actually enforced
findings.description: The module docstring (lines 36-40) and several method/class docstrings assert these round-trip cases are 'marked pytest.mark.xfail(strict=True)' and 'fail today ... post-fix this must pass and the xfail marker must be removed' (e.g. test_triple_quote_content_roundtrips, test_empty_description_roundtrips, TestTortureEndToEnd.test_submodel_nested_torture_roundtrip at :612-614). In reality the Wave 9D fix landed (src/haute/_codegen_builders._sanitize_description docstring at :144-145 states `ast.get_docstring(fn) == desc` now holds), the markers were correctly removed, and the tests PASS. The prose is stale and now lies about the suite's state. This is not a correctness defect (the tests assert the fixed, correct behaviour), but it materially misleads a reader about which invariants are enforced vs aspirational, which is a maintenance hazard in a suite that elsewhere relies on strict-xfail bookkeeping.
findings.evidence: Executed (.venv python -m pytest): test_triple_quote_content_roundtrips, test_empty_description_roundtrips, TestTortureEndToEnd::test_submodel_nested_torture_roundtrip => '3 passed'. No `@pytest.mark.xfail` decorator exists on any of these methods. src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:131-167 confirms the sanitiser now guarantees the round-trip the docstrings call broken.
findings.recommended_fix: Update the module and method docstrings to remove the stale 'xfail(strict=True) / fails today' language and state the invariant is now enforced (the sanitiser guarantees ast.get_docstring == description). No behavioural change to the assertions is needed.

findings.title: No test previews a MULTI-PORT apiInput source node itself, leaving verified bugs V011 + V014 (empty output_columns shadows first-port fallback) completely uncovered
findings.description: The multi-port runtime suite is the only place that exercises 2+ emit-true apiInput tables, but every assertion is on a DOWNSTREAM consumer node (target_node_id="d_policies"/"d_drivers"/"c_policies"/"c_drivers"). The source node 'api' is only ever previewed with a SINGLE-port config (target_node_id="api" appears at lines 149, 248, 337, 438, 447 — all using _single_port_config). The source node's OWN preview when it emits dict[port,DataFrame] is never asserted. That is precisely the code path of two confirmed bugs: V011 (executor.py:1131-1137 _column_infos_for_node: full_output=output_cols.get(node_id) returns the hard-set [] from _execute_lazy.py:1903-1904, and because `[] is not None`, columns=[] and the `elif df is not None` first-port fallback is never reached → the multi-port source reports ZERO columns in its own preview) and V014 (executor.py:1102-1107 _cached_output_names: cached=[] is falsy, falls through to df=eager_outputs.get(node_id) which is a dict, then set(dict.columns) → AttributeError for any instanceOf schema-warning path with a multi-port parent).
findings.evidence: Grep of tests for target_node_id="api" with multi-port: the only 5 hits are all _single_port_config. _execute_lazy.py:1903-1904 hard-sets available_columns[nid]=[] / output_columns[nid]=[] for the multi-port branch; executor.py:1132 `if full_output is not None:` treats the empty list as authoritative. No test asserts results["api"].columns or column_count for a 2-port config, and no test wires a multi-port apiInput into an instanceOf node (the _cached_output_names path).
findings.recommended_fix: Add a test that runs execute_graph(graph, target_node_id="api") with _multi_port_config and asserts the source's own preview exposes a non-empty representative column set (e.g. the first/'policies' port's {policy_id}) and column_count>0 — this fails today (columns==[]) and pins V011. Add a second test wiring a multi-port apiInput as a parent of an instanceOf node so _cached_output_names is exercised; assert no AttributeError and a sensible union-of-ports schema-warning set — pins V014.

findings.title: No test covers V029: the FIRST in-flight reservation is refused when one profile's LIMIT alone exceeds (available_ram - os_reserve); every admission test sizes RAM so the first reservation always fits
findings.description: _reserve_in_flight_budget rejects when `reserved + reservation_bytes > limit_bytes`; with an empty ledger reserved==0 this collapses to `reservation_bytes > limit_bytes` with no first-admission clamp, so on a modest machine (or with a configured per-profile LIMIT larger than available-reserve) the very first heavy job is refused with in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded — the V029 bug. The closest test, test_heavy_execution_admission_counts_in_flight_budget (test_execution_context.py:262), deliberately sets available_ram to 10 GiB so the adaptive OPTIMISER_SETUP budget fits under (10 GiB - 2 GiB reserve); it then needs a SECOND concurrent reservation to trip the cap, and explicitly asserts the FIRST succeeds. test_adaptive_default_memory_budgets_never_exceed_available_ram uses 384 MiB but calls execution_budget_for_profile (never the admission/_reserve_in_flight_budget path). So the single-heavy-job boundary is untested.
findings.evidence: Every available_ram_bytes monkeypatch in the admission tests is 10/16/20/64 GiB (test_execution_context.py:117,146,158,173,186,213,251,269-270,305-306,326,346,366). _in_flight_limit_bytes = max(available - reserve, 1) (admission.py:546-555); the guard at admission.py:513 has no `reserved > 0` clamp. No test drives create_admitted_execution_context with available_ram small enough (or HAUTE_*_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB large enough) that a single profile reservation exceeds limit_bytes on an empty ledger.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a test that clears in-flight reservations, sets available_ram_bytes to e.g. 1 GiB (or sets HAUTE_OPTIMISER_SETUP_MEMORY_LIMIT_MB above available-reserve) and asserts the FIRST create_admitted_execution_context(profile=OPTIMISER_SETUP) is admitted (a single heavy job must run) — this fails today with ExecutionAdmissionError(reason='in_flight_memory_budget_exceeded'), pinning V029. Pair with the fix that only enforces the cap when reserved>0.

findings.location: tests/test_worker_isolation.py:47-51 (test_isolated_worker_returns_picklable_value) — only tiny payloads tested anywhere in the file
findings.title: No test returns a multi-MiB payload from run_isolated_worker, leaving verified deadlock V036 (mp.Queue feeder-pipe deadlock: parent joins child before draining the result queue) uncovered
findings.description: V036: run_isolated_worker / _wait_for_worker join the child to completion BEFORE reading result_queue; with multiprocessing.Queue a put() larger than the OS pipe buffer (~64 KiB) blocks the child's feeder thread on the pipe write until the parent reads, but the parent only join()s — classic feeder-pipe deadlock that hangs at interpreter shutdown. Every worker_isolation test returns a tiny dict ({"sum": ...}, soft/hard rlimit ints, {"sum": 6}) — all well under the pipe buffer, so the deadlock can never trigger. The supervisor tests (lines 170-228) likewise return tiny results. There is no large-result regression.
findings.evidence: Grep for multi-MiB / 64*1024 / cancel_join_thread / feeder / large payload in test_worker_isolation.py: no matches. The largest returned object in the file is a small dict or a 2-tuple of ints.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a TDD regression: run_isolated_worker(fn) where fn returns a payload exceeding the pipe buffer (e.g. b"\0" * (4 * 1024 * 1024) or a list of ~1M ints), wrapped in pytest with a hard timeout (e.g. via a watchdog thread or asyncio.wait_for in an isolated harness), asserting it returns rather than hanging. This fails (hangs) today and pins V036; the fix drains the queue concurrently or calls result_queue.cancel_join_thread() in the child.

findings.title: Continuous-banding NaN/Inf tests assert only the band OUTPUT column and never the source column, so verified bug V025 (source float column silently overwritten, destroying NaN/Inf for downstream) is uncovered and the tests give false confidence
findings.description: V025: in the continuous path _apply_banding rewrites the SOURCE column with `pl.when(col.is_nan()|col.is_infinite()).then(None).otherwise(col).alias(column)` (note .alias(column) — same name, not a temp), so the returned frame's source column has every NaN/+/-Inf replaced by null for all downstream nodes. The two NaN/Inf tests build df with NaN/Inf in column 'x' and assert only result["band"] (the output) is correct; they never assert result["x"] still contains the original NaN/Inf. Because the band output is computed correctly regardless, these tests pass while the silent source-column corruption goes undetected. This flows through both the eager executor and the chunk path (banding is used in _chunk_safe_graph), but the chunk==full proofs use with_columns, not banding, so they don't catch it either.
findings.evidence: _rating.py:110-116 assigns the sanitised expression back via .alias(column) onto the input column and reassigns lf. test_banding.py:933-937 and 946-950 assert only bands = result["band"].to_list(); no assertion on result["x"].
findings.recommended_fix: Extend test_nan_input_falls_to_default / test_inf_input_falls_to_default (or add a sibling) to assert the returned frame's SOURCE column is unchanged: result["x"] still has NaN at index 1 (and +/-Inf preserved), in addition to the band assertions. This fails today (x[1] becomes null), pinning V025; the fix builds the sanitised expr into a local/temp rather than aliasing onto the source.

findings.title: No test drives the V101 permit double-release path (acquire_task AND superseded_task both in `done` in the same step); the existing RacingLimiter test makes acquire block forever so the both-done branch is never hit
findings.description: V101: when asyncio.wait(FIRST_COMPLETED) returns with BOTH acquire_task and superseded_task done (reachable whenever a permit is available exactly when the request is superseded), the body releases the just-acquired permit at L184 (acquired=False), raises SupersededRequestError, and the except handler then re-derives acquired=True at L191-192 from the drained acquire result (which has no memory that L184 already released) and releases AGAIN at L195 → permit leak. The dedicated test test_superseded_limiter_acquire_race_releases_slot uses a RacingLimiter whose first acquire() blocks until cancelled, so acquire_task is NEVER in `done` alongside superseded_task — the both-done branch (the actual bug locus) is never exercised. (Its `limiter.releases == 2` assertion is correct accounting for the drain-then-release path and is NOT codifying the leak.)
findings.evidence: RacingLimiter.acquire (test_request_supersession.py:198-205) awaits asyncio.Event().wait() on the first call, guaranteeing the acquire task stays pending until cancelled in the except handler; thus `if acquire_task in done` (supersession.py:176) is False on the FIRST_COMPLETED return. No test provides a limiter that is immediately acquirable AND arranges supersession in the same loop step so both tasks complete together.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a test with a real asyncio.Semaphore(1) that is free, where the request is marked superseded (bump latest_generation) before the await asyncio.wait resolves, so both acquire_task and superseded_task are done together; assert the semaphore's value returns to its initial count (no net leak) after the SupersededRequestError. This fails today (double release → value 2 on a Semaphore(1)) and pins V101.

findings.title: Banding chunk-equivalence tests compare chunked-vs-full where BOTH paths share the same buggy banding (V025), so an oracle that is itself wrong cannot detect source-column corruption
findings.description: The chunk-safe-chain equivalence tests use a graph whose first transform is continuous banding on column 'age', then assert plt.assert_frame_equal(chunked, full). Because both the chunked and the full path call the same _apply_banding (which mutates the source 'age' column per V025), the differential oracle agrees and the corruption is invisible. The output node selects age_band (not raw age), so even the value of the mutated column is dropped before assertion. This is acceptable as an equivalence test but should not be relied on as evidence that banding preserves source columns; the explicit V025 pin (separate finding) is what is missing.
findings.evidence: _chunk_safe_graph (test_chunk_runner.py:68-126) routes age through a continuous 'banding' node; DEFAULT_OUTPUT_FIELDS excludes raw 'age'. The whitelist chunk==full proofs (test_chunk_whitelist_proofs.py) cover with_columns/expr/fn constructs but deliberately do NOT include banding, so neither suite asserts banding preserves the input float column.
findings.recommended_fix: Keep these equivalence tests, but do not treat them as banding-correctness evidence. Add the dedicated V025 source-column-preservation assertion in test_banding.py (see the V025 finding) which is independent of the chunk oracle.

findings.location: tests/test_scalar_array_and_inference.py:59-83 (and the inference suite as a whole); gap relative to src/haute/_json_shred.py:1199-1221
findings.title: No test for a literal JSON key named "$value" — inference + shred silently drop EVERY record of that table (V015)
findings.description: Verified bug V015: the module reserves the leaf token `$value` (`_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF`) and the header comment at _json_shred.py:70-71 asserts "a JSON key can't be `$value` in this path grammar" — which is false. `infer_v2_schema_from_data` builds object columns as `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` (line 1214) with NO escaping, so a record carrying a real key `"$value"` produces an object-table column with path `$[*].$value`; at shred time the leaf equals the scalar-array sentinel and the object-table branch drops every row. The whole inference suite (test_scalar_array_and_inference.py, test_v2_codec_and_shred.py, test_json_shred_properties.py) never constructs a record with a key literally named `$value`, so this catastrophic silent-data-loss path on the pricing-critical JSON ingestion route is entirely untested.
findings.evidence: Reproduced with the project venv: infer_v2_schema_from_data on [{"$value":10,"id":1},{"$value":20,"id":2}] yields root cols [('$value','$[*].$value'),('id','$[*].id')]; shred_to_buffers(data, schema) returns {'$[*]': []} — ZERO rows from two records. The reserved-sentinel guard at _json_shred.py:610/629/636 treats the real key as the scalar sentinel and the object-table shape check drops all records. Grep confirms no test references `$value` as a literal data key. VERIFIED-BUGS.md V015 (repro review/04-exhaustive/repro/V015.py).
findings.recommended_fix: Add a failing test (TDD) feeding records with a real key `"$value"` and asserting either a loud ApiInputSchemaError at validate/inference time (preferred per the fail-loud rule) or correct emission of the value — never a silent empty buffer. Pair with the source fix in validate_v2_schema that raises when a parsed leaf equals `_SCALAR_VALUE_LEAF` on a non-scalar table. The same test must assert shred_to_buffers row count == record count for that table.

findings.title: No test for a literal JSON key containing a dot (e.g. "a.b") — inference manufactures a dotted path and shred silently resolves the value to None (V016)
findings.description: Verified bug V016: inference emits an object column path `f"{table_path}.{col_name}"` with no escaping, so a record key `"a.b"` yields column path `$[*].a.b`. `parse_column_path` returns leaf `a.b`, which `_resolve_leaf` (lines 526-533) interprets as a NESTED walk (`value.get('a').get('b')`), absent for the flat key, so the column resolves to None — the value is silently lost and the row is still emitted (not even counted as a skip). The existing dotted-leaf tests (lines 330, 359) pin only the LEGITIMATE nested-path feature; there is no test for the ambiguous case where the dotted segment is a real flat key, so the silent corruption is uncovered.
findings.evidence: Reproduced with the project venv: infer + shred on [{"a.b":42,"id":1}] produces column path `$[*].a.b` and shred_to_buffers returns [{'a.b': None, 'id': 1}] — the original value 42 is gone, no skip recorded. VERIFIED-BUGS.md V016 (repro review/04-exhaustive/repro/V016.py). The legitimate-feature tests at lines 330/359 confirm the dotted-as-nested design that creates the ambiguity, but none cover a literal-dot key.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a failing test feeding a record with a literal-dot key and assert a loud failure (ApiInputSchemaError naming the column at validate/infer time) rather than a None value, consistent with the codebase fail-loud rule. The fix must disambiguate flat-key vs nested-path (escape the key in the inferred path, or reject a leaf containing '.' when no intermediate object table exists).

findings.title: Shred conservation property tests cannot catch the nested-list scalar-array row-inflation bug — strategy excludes nested lists and the object-table test pre-flattens them into the expected count (catalog finding #4)
findings.description: Confirmed high-severity bug (review/02-findings/catalog.md #4): for a scalar child table, `_walk` recurses unconditionally into nested-list elements (_json_shred.py:600-617), so `{"tags":["a",["b","c"],"d"]}` emits 4 rows from 3 source elements with zero skip accounting — a silent conservation-law violation with no provenance. The scalar-child property test at line 72-107 has the correct 1-row-per-element assertion but draws elements from `st.one_of(st.text(max_size=5), st.none())` (line 77), DELIBERATELY excluding nested lists, so it never exercises the bug. The object-array conservation test (122-169) at line 161-163 computes its expected `visited` count by FLATTENING nested lists (`visited += len(el) if isinstance(el, list) else 1`) — it bakes the flatten semantics into the expected value, so an inflation-by-flattening defect cannot fail it; the test accommodates the buggy behaviour instead of asserting elements map 1:1.
findings.evidence: catalog.md #4 line 70 states verbatim: 'the scalar-child conservation property test tests/test_json_shred_properties.py:72-107 has the correct assertion ... but draws tags elements from st.one_of(st.text(max_size=5), st.none()) at line 77 — nested lists excluded, so it never exercises this case.' Repro cache__shred-nested-list-scalar-array-row-inflation.py: emitted [a,b,c,d] (4) from a 3-element array, skip stats {records:0, rows_by_table:{}}, conservation 4+0 != 3. Source confirmed at _json_shred.py:617 (`_walk(item, current_path)` with no shape guard).
findings.recommended_fix: Extend the scalar-child element strategy (line 77) to include nested lists (`st.lists(...)`), or add a focused regression asserting emitted + skipped == element_count for {"tags":["a",["b","c"],"d"]} (counting the nested list as ONE malformed element/skip, not its flattened leaves). Stop deriving the object-array test's expected count by flattening nested lists; assert a nested-list element contributes exactly one skip. Fix _walk to count a list element as a single skipped row rather than recursing.

findings.location: tests/test_caching_correctness.py:232-320 (TestFingerprintEdgeHandleSensitivity) and tests/test_graph_fingerprint_cached.py:156-199 (TestExtraKeysAreNotCached); gap relative to src/haute/_cache.py:429-432
findings.title: graph_fingerprint extra_keys join is non-injective (newline collision) and untested — the edge-handle tests carefully cover separator collisions but the extra_keys path was left unframed (V035 residual)
findings.description: Verified bug V035 was only PARTIALLY fixed: node lines and edges are now framed via `canonical_json` (_cache.py:200,214), but `graph_fingerprint` still joins extra_keys/context with a bare `"\n".join([*extra_keys, *context_parts, base])` (line 431), which is non-injective. The test suite has thorough separator/None/null collision coverage for EDGES (TestFingerprintEdgeHandleSensitivity, including test_none_handle_differs_from_handle_named_like_null) but NO equivalent injectivity test for extra_keys: TestExtraKeysAreNotCached only checks ordering sensitivity ((a,b) != (b,a)) and that extras don't poison the base. This residual is reachable in production because extra_keys carry unvalidated node IDs: deploy/_schema.py:95 `graph_fingerprint(graph, output_node_id, *input_node_ids)` and trace.py:381 `graph_fingerprint(graph, target_node_id, ...)`; GraphNode.id has no validator (per V035), so a node id containing a newline collides two structurally different fingerprint inputs → wrong cached deploy schema / trace.
findings.evidence: Reproduced with the project venv: graph_fingerprint(g, "a", "b") == graph_fingerprint(g, "a\nb") (both v5:7a01570ba0435ca9). Source confirmed: _cache.py:431 unframed newline join. Callers confirmed: deploy/_schema.py:95, trace.py:381,417,432, executor.py:905. VERIFIED-BUGS.md V035 (repro V035.py). The edge tests show the codebase KNOWS this class of bug (it framed edges) but did not extend the guard to extra_keys.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a regression asserting graph_fingerprint(g, 'a', 'b') != graph_fingerprint(g, 'a\nb') (and a node-id-with-newline variant through the deploy/trace call shape). Fix the source by framing the extra_keys/context join with canonical_json (mirroring the edge fix) so the combined key is injective.

findings.title: canonical_json set order-independence is untested for NaN floats, and is in fact non-deterministic there (V034) — the property test deliberately excludes NaN
findings.description: Verified bug V034: canonical_json's documented contract (_cache.py:81-99, 119-123) promises sets/frozensets encode identically regardless of insertion order. `_sort_key` maps every float including NaN to `("2_num", value)` (lines 176-177); because all NaN comparisons are False, Python's stable sort cannot order NaN against finite numbers, so a set mixing NaN and finite values canonicalises differently depending on the set's internal iteration order. The property test test_set_insertion_order_is_irrelevant explicitly excludes NaN (`_canonical_scalars` uses `st.floats(allow_nan=False)`, lines 506-512). The exclusion is justified for value-equality assertions, but it leaves the order-independence invariant UNTESTED at exactly the input where it is broken — and non-finite floats are legitimate digest material here (open banding bounds; the suite even pins canonical_json(float('inf'))=='Infinity' at line 470).
findings.evidence: Reproduced with the project venv over randomized insertion orders: the logical set {1.0, 38.0, 4xNaN} canonicalises to BOTH '{"s":[1.0,NaN,38.0,NaN,NaN,NaN]}' and '{"s":[1.0,38.0,NaN,NaN,NaN,NaN]}' — same set, two digests. _sort_key(nan) == ('2_num', nan). VERIFIED-BUGS.md V034 (repro V034.py). Test exclusion at test_caching_correctness.py:504-512.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a property/example test asserting canonical_json of a NaN-containing set is identical across insertion orders (and that NaN sorts to a fixed position). Fix _sort_key to give non-finite floats a deterministic secondary key (e.g. NaN -> ('2_num_nan', 0)) so all NaN collapse identically and order after finite values.

findings.title: test_cache_hit endorses the graph_fingerprint-keyed output-schema short-circuit even though the key excludes model-artifact identity (catalog finding #8 / V8)
findings.description: Confirmed high-severity bug (catalog.md #8): infer_output_schema caches the dry-run output schema keyed on graph_fingerprint(graph, output_node_id, *input_node_ids), which hashes only node configs + edge topology + preamble + utility source — NOT model-artifact bytes or the resolved MLflow version. After a modelScore model swap (registered 'latest' retrain, or in-place run-artifact retrain) the fingerprint is byte-identical, so a stale schema is reused and baked into the MLflow ModelSignature / deploy manifest. test_cache_hit pre-writes a cache entry under graph_fingerprint(graph,'out','src') and asserts score_graph is NOT called and the cached schema is returned — it pins the very short-circuit that causes the stale-schema bug, using a graph with NO modelScore node so the defect is invisible. When V8 is fixed (fold artifact identity into the key), this test must change.
findings.evidence: catalog.md #8 line 113 states verbatim: 'tests/test_deploy_internals.py::test_cache_hit (481-528) explicitly endorses the fingerprint-keyed short-circuit and never exercises a model-artifact swap.' Confirmed by reading the test: it asserts mock_score.assert_not_called() and result == cached schema, with no modelScore node and no artifact-swap scenario. Repro platform__deploy-output-schema-cache-misses-model-artifact.py shows the fingerprint is byte-identical across a model swap and the cache returns the stale dtype.
findings.recommended_fix: Keep a (renamed) test that pins the cache hit only for graphs with NO artifact-bearing nodes, and ADD a regression that uses a modelScore node, seeds the cache, swaps the artifact bytes/version without editing config, and asserts the recomputed (not stale) schema is returned. This forces the source fix to fold resolved-artifact/version identity into the output-schema cache key.

findings.title: Volatile-wins-over-disk dispatch test only asserts HTTP 200, never verifies that the volatile schema actually won
findings.description: The test's stated purpose is to prove that when both volatile_schema and config_path are supplied, the in-memory volatile schema wins over the on-disk one (the _select_v2_config volatile arm). It seeds an on-disk config whose column is named 'wrong' and a volatile config whose column is named 'x', but then asserts ONLY `resp.status_code == 200` (with a comment conceding 'cached: false is fine'). Both the volatile-wins and the disk-wins (and even a no-dispatch) outcomes return 200/cached:false here, so the assertion cannot distinguish them — the test would pass even if the dispatch silently chose the wrong source. It exercises the line for coverage without verifying the behaviour.
findings.evidence: test body lines 623-651: the on-disk 'wrong' vs volatile 'x' divergence is set up specifically to be observable, but the only assertion is status_code == 200; the inline comment acknowledges the behaviour is not asserted ('Behaviour we care about is "did it dispatch via volatile" — cached: false is fine').
findings.recommended_fix: Make the outcome observable and assert it: e.g. build with the volatile schema first (so a cache exists matching the volatile fingerprint), then POST /status with both sources and assert cached is True under the volatile schema while a disk-only call returns cached False — or assert the returned column_count/schema reflects the volatile ('x') schema, not the disk ('wrong') schema.

findings.title: FingerprintCache concurrency test only checks the result is a dict, so it cannot detect torn/inconsistent slot state
findings.description: The concurrency test runs two writers (both storing the SAME fingerprint 'fp1' with `{"a": i}` payloads) and two readers, but the reader's only check is `if result is not None and not isinstance(result, dict): errors.append(...)`. Because all writers use the same key and a dict value, the only failure this can catch is a non-dict return or an exception. It never asserts internal consistency (e.g. that a returned multi-slot entry is coherent, that the inner value is one of the stored payloads, or that size never exceeds max_entries), so a partially-published or interleaved entry would pass. This is a smoke test masquerading as a thread-safety guarantee.
findings.evidence: test body lines 195-210: reader asserts only isinstance(result, dict); writers all use fp='fp1'. No assertion on the inner payload identity, slot coherence, or cache size invariants.
findings.recommended_fix: Strengthen the readers to assert the returned entry is internally coherent: store DISTINCT keys per writer with a checksum relationship between slots (e.g. slot_b == f(slot_a)) and assert the relationship holds on every read, and assert len(cache) never exceeds max_entries. This turns the test into a real torn-state detector.

findings.title: No test pins that continuous banding leaves the SOURCE float column untouched (V025: _apply_banding silently overwrites NaN/Inf on the input column for all downstream nodes)
findings.description: VERIFIED-BUGS V025 (src/haute/_rating.py:104-116) is live: in the continuous path, when the banded column is Float32/Float64, _apply_banding sanitises NaN/Inf by `lf = lf.with_columns(pl.when(col.is_nan()|col.is_infinite()).then(None).otherwise(col).alias(column))` — aliasing the sanitised expression back onto the SAME source column name. Every NaN/+/-Inf in the input factor is permanently replaced with null in the returned frame, a pure side-effect on a column the node was only supposed to READ. Any downstream node (or the user's own later use of that column) silently loses NaN/Inf. The entire banding test suite exercises only the OUTPUT band column. The closest tests actively dodge the bug: test_continuous_banding_integer_column uses an Int column (col_dtype not in (Float32,Float64), so the mutation branch is never taken), and test_inf_values_in_input / test_inf_input_falls_to_default assert only result['band'] (the output), never that result['x'] still contains inf/-inf. So the mutation is completely unguarded by tests on a pricing-critical path.
findings.evidence: Source: src/haute/_rating.py:109-116 `if col_dtype in (pl.Float32, pl.Float64): lf = lf.with_columns(pl.when(col.is_nan()|col.is_infinite()).then(pl.lit(None)).otherwise(col).alias(column)); col = pl.col(column)`. test_banding.py:946-950 asserts `result['band'][1] == 'dflt'` etc but never re-reads result['x']; the input inf/-inf are gone from x and no assertion catches it. No test in tests/test_banding.py or tests/test_rating.py reads back the SOURCE column after a Float banding to confirm NaN/Inf survived.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a failing test (TDD for the V025 fix): build a Float64 column containing [1.0, nan, inf, -inf], apply continuous banding to a DIFFERENT output column, then assert BOTH that the band output is correct AND that the source column is byte-identical to the input (e.g. via polars.testing.assert_series_equal on result['x'] vs the original, checking is_nan()/is_infinite() counts are preserved). The fix (sanitise into a temp expr/column, never alias onto `column`) then makes it pass. Add the Float32 variant too.

findings.title: Banding column-contract is never tested for the empty-rules factor (V012: _banding_columns declares an outputColumn the runtime never produces, so projection prunes a needed upstream column)
findings.description: VERIFIED-BUGS V012 (src/haute/_builders.py:760-764) is live: `_banding_columns` returns `produced = {f['outputColumn'] for f in factors if f.get('outputColumn')}` with NO rules-guard, while the runtime `_apply_banding_factors` (src/haute/_rating.py:240-245) skips any factor where `not col or not out or not rules`. A banding factor with column+outputColumn set but empty/absent `rules` is therefore DECLARED as produced by the contract yet never created at runtime. projection demand-propagation subtracts produced columns from upstream demand, so it can prune a column the parent actually needed — a real (not display-only) wrong-output path in batch/deploy. Every banding-contract test passes factors that HAVE rules: test_banding_codegen_includes_contract_kwarg uses rules=[{...}], the round-trip test at :312-320 uses a non-empty rules list, and _minimal_config_for builds a 'representative' config (also rules-bearing). The empty-rules divergence between contract and runtime is entirely uncovered.
findings.evidence: Contract: src/haute/_builders.py:762 `produced = {f['outputColumn'] for f in factors if f.get('outputColumn')}` (no rules check). Runtime: src/haute/_rating.py:243-245 `rules = factor.get('rules', []) or []; if not col or not out or not rules: continue`. Test gap: test_column_contracts_adoption.py:253 rules=[{'max':25,'value':'0'}]; :317 rules=[{'op1':'<=','val1':'25','assignment':'0'}] — both non-empty. No test asserts get_column_contract('banding', {factors:[{column:'age', outputColumn:'age_band', rules:[]}]}) produces ({}, ...) to match the runtime skip.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a contract-vs-runtime parity test: for a banding factor with column+outputColumn but rules=[], assert _banding_columns/get_column_contract yields produced == set() (matching _apply_banding_factors' skip), and ideally an end-to-end projection test asserting the upstream `column` is NOT pruned. This both pins V012 and forces the fix to normalise+guard rules in _banding_columns.

findings.title: Float32 enrichment divergence (catalog #11) is codified as 'out of scope' by the test contract, not fixed — the actuary trace can show a wrong matched/default flag for non-integer Float32 factors
findings.description: catalog #11 (src/haute/_rating.py:309-343 mirror vs 346-370 twin) is a verified medium bug: for a non-integer Float32 factor value (e.g. 0.1), the engine twin _rating_key_expr casts the Float32 column to Utf8 giving '0.1' (and MATCHES), but the Python mirror normalise_rating_key receives the already-widened f64 image (0.10000000149011612) and formats '0.10000000149011612'. Trace enrichment (_trace_enrichment) uses the mirror to decide matched/default, so a row the engine MATCHED is shown to the actuary as no_match/default — a self-contradictory waterfall flag. The test file's docstring (lines 24-26) explicitly states 'Float32 columns lose their dtype at the trace JSON boundary, so non-integer Float32 keys are outside the enrichment-agreement guarantee', and the two Float32 tests (lines 177-199) assert ONLY the engine match (out['f'] == [2.0]/[9.0]) — never enrichment agreement. The strong assert_engine_and_enrichment_agree harness (lines 542-578) is never called with a Float32 frame. So the suite pins the buggy carve-out as intended behaviour: a known-wrong trace flag is documented as 'not guaranteed' rather than caught.
findings.evidence: test_rating_key_agreement.py:24-26 docstring carving out Float32; lines 184,197 use dtype=pl.Float32 but assert only out['f'].to_list(); grep confirms assert_engine_and_enrichment_agree is never invoked with a Float32 series (the dtype=pl.Float32 occurrences are 184 and 197 only, both engine-match-only). catalog #11 evidence: 'the two existing Float32 tests (lines 177,189) assert only the engine match, never enrichment agreement, so the path is unguarded and untested.'
findings.recommended_fix: Add an enrichment-agreement test that calls assert_engine_and_enrichment_agree with a non-integer Float32 frame (e.g. score Float32 0.1 vs entry key 0.1) — it fails today, exposing the wrong waterfall flag. Pair with the catalog #11 fix (thread the factor's original dtype into _enrich_single_table and canonicalise the observed cell + entry key in that dtype) and update the docstring to remove the Float32 exclusion once the fix lands.

findings.title: test_breakpoints_only_open_ended pins SILENT data loss: a single open-ended breakpoint (the user's catch-all label) is dropped, producing zero rules
findings.description: _breakpoints_to_rules only appends the open-ended tail rule `if open_ended is not None and prev_boundary is not None` (src/haute/_rating.py:213). When the user configures a breakpoints factor whose ONLY entry is an open-ended catch-all (boundary='', label='All') — a natural way to say 'everything is band X' — there is no prior bounded boundary, so the open-ended rule is silently discarded and the factor produces NO band column at all (chain is None -> frame returned unchanged). The test asserts exactly this as correct: `assert rules == []` with the comment 'open-ended is skipped'. Per CLAUDE.md's fail-loud / no-silent-loss mandate this is a silent data-loss bug being codified as intended: the actuary's catch-all label vanishes with no error, and the banding output column the rest of the pipeline expects is never created. Compare the loud handling of duplicate/non-numeric boundaries elsewhere in the same class — only the all-rows catch-all is silently swallowed.
findings.evidence: src/haute/_rating.py:213 `if open_ended is not None and prev_boundary is not None:` — open-ended without a bounded predecessor is dropped. test_banding.py:1088-1093 `breakpoints = [{'boundary':'','label':'All'}]; rules = _breakpoints_to_rules(breakpoints); assert rules == []`. Downstream: _apply_banding with empty rules returns the frame unchanged (no output column), so a single-catch-all breakpoints factor is a no-op.
findings.recommended_fix: Decide the intended contract and pin it loudly: either (a) a lone open-ended breakpoint should produce a single unconditional rule assigning every row to its label (change _breakpoints_to_rules to emit it and update the test to assert the band is applied), or (b) it is a config error and should raise ValueError naming the factor. Either way replace the `assert rules == []` 'silently skipped' expectation, which currently blesses dropping the user's only label.

findings.title: test_combine_with_inf asserts Polars' own float arithmetic (inf*2==inf) rather than any haute behaviour
findings.description: test_combine_with_inf builds a finite-and-inf input and asserts `inf * 2.0 == inf` and `inf + 2.0 == inf`. _combine_rating_columns for the multiply/add path is a thin pl.fold over the columns; the assertion is just IEEE-754 float semantics that Polars provides, not a property of the rating-combine logic (no null-handling, no neutral-element, no operation dispatch is exercised by the inf value specifically — those are covered by other tests). It adds maintenance surface without testing haute. Low severity (it isn't wrong, just non-load-bearing), flagged only because the surrounding class title 'ExtremeFloatValues' implies it guards a pricing edge it doesn't.
findings.evidence: test_rating.py:1221-1225 `result_mul = _combine_rating_columns(lf, ['a','b'], 'multiply', 'out').collect(); assert result_mul['out'].to_list() == [float('inf')]` — a is inf, b is 2.0. The only haute-specific risk on this path (inf entering a combined PREMIUM and silently producing inf pricing) is not asserted as undesirable anywhere; the test instead blesses inf propagation.
findings.recommended_fix: Either delete (redundant with IEEE semantics) or, more valuably, turn it into a real guard: assert that an inf appearing in a COMBINED rating output (e.g. premium) is surfaced/rejected rather than silently propagated as inf, consistent with the entry-value NaN/Inf rejection already enforced at test_rating.py:1188-1200.

findings.title: Schema-call-count test over-mocks the unit under test and asserts an implementation detail with a loose bound that hides regressions
findings.description: This P4 performance test wraps the LazyFrame in a _SchemaCountingLF proxy and asserts `call_counter.call_count <= 2`. (1) It is testing an internal optimisation (how many times collect_schema is called) rather than observable behaviour, which is brittle. (2) The bound is `<= 2`, and the inline comment admits 'Schema is called twice', so the assertion would still pass if a regression dropped the per-factor caching down to 1 call OR if some unrelated refactor called it 0 times — it only catches an INCREASE past 2. The named intent ('called exactly once, not per-factor') is not what is asserted; with 3 factors a per-factor regression would be 3 (caught), but the off-by-one fuzz (<=2 vs ==1) means the test no longer pins the stated contract. The companion test_existing_cols_computed_once_for_lazy asserts nothing about call counts at all (just the result values), so it does not back-stop this.
findings.evidence: test_rating.py:565-567 `assert call_counter.call_count <= 2, (...'expected at most 2')` with comment at 564 'Schema is called twice: once for existing_cols check, once for dtype preservation'. The class/method names say 'called exactly once' / 'not per-factor' but the assertion permits 0,1,2.
findings.recommended_fix: Assert the exact expected count (==2 given the documented two call sites, or ==1 if the contract truly is once) so a drift in either direction is caught; or, better, drop the proxy and assert the observable consequence (correct dtype preservation + correct values) which the sibling test already does, removing the brittle white-box count.

findings.title: try/except 'either outcome acceptable' tests assert almost nothing and would pass even if string columns silently produced wrong numeric pricing
findings.description: These tests run a rating-combine over string columns inside try/except where the except branch is a bare `pass` ('Raising is also acceptable'). The only thing actually asserted is that, IF no exception is raised, the result equals a specific concatenation/lexicographic value. If the implementation instead silently coerced strings to 0.0 and raised nothing, the success branch's assert would fire and fail — but if it raised ANY exception (even an unrelated/wrong one), the except swallows it and the test passes. So the test does not actually pin the stated guarantee ('does NOT silently return 0'): a wrong-but-raising implementation passes vacuously. For a pricing engine, 'multiply/add on a mistyped string column' is exactly the silent-corruption class CLAUDE.md calls out.
findings.evidence: test_rating.py:834-839 `try: result = _combine_rating_columns(...,'add',...).collect(); assert result['out'].to_list() == ['helloworld'] except Exception: pass`. Same shape at 844-850 for min/max. The docstring claims 'the key is it does NOT silently return 0' yet no assertion runs in the except path to verify the failure was a clean type error rather than e.g. a silent 0.
findings.recommended_fix: Replace the broad try/except with an explicit expectation: assert pytest.raises(<the specific Polars error type>) for multiply on strings (the genuinely unsupported case), and for add assert the exact concatenation if that is the supported contract. Remove the bare-pass except so a wrong-but-raising or silent-0 implementation cannot pass vacuously.

findings.title: Test pins the legacy frontier_min/frontier_max broadcast-to-every-constraint bug (#44) as correct
findings.description: Catalog finding #44 confirms _auto_frontier_ranges_from_config silently broadcasts a single scalar (frontier_min, frontier_max) absolute interval to EVERY constraint regardless of scale, producing a frontier swept over a wildly wrong threshold range for all-but-one constraint. This test sets up a 2-constraint config (volume with min 0.9 and loss with max 20.0) carrying only the scalar pair frontier_min=10.0 / frontier_max=20.0, and asserts status 200 plus mock_solver.frontier.call_args.kwargs['threshold_ranges'] == {'volume': (10.0, 20.0), 'loss': (10.0, 20.0)} — i.e. it asserts the identical interval applied to two differently-scaled constraints is the intended contract. The catalog fix explicitly states: 'update test_frontier_without_ranges_uses_config_absolute_ranges, which currently codifies the broadcast as correct.' This test must be changed in lockstep with the fix (multi-constraint + scalar-only should raise) or it will block it and continue to bless silently-misconfigured frontiers.
findings.evidence: Lines 5163-5166 config: constraints={'volume':{'min':0.9},'loss':{'max':20.0}}, frontier_min=10.0, frontier_max=20.0. Lines 5182-5185 assert threshold_ranges == {'volume': (10.0, 20.0), 'loss': (10.0, 20.0)}. Catalog #44: 'Add a failing test that a 2-constraint config with only frontier_min/frontier_max now raises (and update test_frontier_without_ranges_uses_config_absolute_ranges, which currently codifies the broadcast as correct).'
findings.recommended_fix: When the bug is fixed, change this test so a multi-constraint config with only the scalar frontier_min/frontier_max asserts a loud ValueError/4xx instructing the user to supply per-constraint frontier_ranges; retain a separate single-constraint scalar test for the backward-compatible path. Do not leave the 2-constraint broadcast asserted as success.

findings.title: Ratebook frontier-point save tests bake in the re-solve-vs-displayed-point divergence (#16) and pin the re-solve total as authoritative
findings.description: Catalog finding #16 (medium, executed-repro) confirms _materialise_ratebook_frontier_point re-solves coordinate descent warm-started from the stored point's lambdas instead of reusing the sweep's recorded optimum, so the SAVED/DEPLOYED factor tables and totals can disagree with the frontier row the user clicked. The test fixture deliberately makes the displayed frontier point (total_objective=220.0, total_volume=0.97 via _frontier_point_summary) DIFFER from the mocked re-solve output (_ratebook_solve_result_namespace total_objective=222.0, factor tables {North:1.08, South:0.92}). The save test then asserts saved['total_objective'] == 222.0 and saved['factor_tables'] == _expected_region_factor_tables() — i.e. it pins the RE-SOLVE value (222.0), not the displayed point (220.0), as the saved/deployed artifact. No test anywhere asserts the re-solve reproduces the displayed point within tolerance. Worse, because the solver is mocked with a fixed return_value, this test architecture is structurally incapable of catching the real divergence the repro demonstrated (displayed 1.10 relativity saved as 0.80, a 27% mispricing that violated the selected cost ceiling). The companion select test (9650, test_select_ratebook_frontier_point_does_not_reuse_base_factor_tables) asserts the fast-path summary shows 220.0, cementing that the same job legitimately shows 220 on screen and saves 222 to disk.
findings.evidence: Fixture _frontier_point_summary used in _make_ratebook_frontier_materialisation_job:4700-4705 => total_objective=220.0, total_volume=0.97. Mock solver.solve.return_value=_ratebook_solve_result_namespace() => total_objective=222.0 (line 4621), factor_tables {North:1.08,South:0.92} (4655). Save test asserts saved['total_objective']==222.0 (9311) and factor_tables==_expected_region_factor_tables() (9313). Select test asserts job['result']['total_objective']==220.0 (9669). Catalog #16 fix: 'add a loud consistency check: assert the re-solve's total_objective and each total_<name> reproduce the stored frontier row within cd_tolerance ... before persisting; on mismatch, fail loudly'.
findings.recommended_fix: Add a real-solver consistency test (no mock) that selects/saves a ratebook frontier point and asserts the saved total_objective, each total_<constraint>, and factor-table values reproduce the displayed frontier-row values within cd_tolerance. When #16 is fixed, update these mocked tests so the fixture's displayed point and re-solve output agree (or assert the new fail-loud-on-divergence behaviour) rather than blessing 220-displayed / 222-saved as intended.

findings.title: Only real-solver ratebook frontier-point save/select test asserts shapes/types, never numeric agreement with the displayed point (misses #16)
findings.description: This is the single real-library (un-mocked) test that exercises ratebook frontier-point select + save end-to-end, so it is the only test that COULD catch the #16 re-solve divergence. But it asserts only structural/type properties: set(tables)=={'region'}, the three group names {North,South,East}, that optimal_scenario_value is a float, quote_count==3, that cd_iterations/clamp_rate are int/float, saved['mode']=='ratebook', lambdas is a dict, converged is a bool, iterations is an int. It never compares the saved total_objective / total_constraints / factor relativity VALUES against the frontier point row the user selected (point_index 0). A re-solve that converges to a different stationary point with different factor values and a constraint-ceiling violation would still satisfy every assertion here. This is exactly the consistency check catalog #16 says is absent, and it leaves the highest-value real-solver path blind to a per-quote mispricing of the deployed artifact.
findings.evidence: Assertions at 432-440 (group names, float type, quote_count==3, cd_iterations/clamp_rate types) and 453-463 (mode, lambdas is dict, converged is bool, iterations is int, factor group names). No assertion on saved['total_objective'], saved['total_constraints'], or any optimal_scenario_value numeric value vs the frontier point selected. Catalog #16 notes 'NO consistency guard exists ... it never compares the re-solved totals/constraints/tables against the displayed frontier row'.
findings.recommended_fix: Strengthen this test (or add a sibling) to read the displayed frontier point (from the /frontier response points[0]) and assert the saved total_objective, each total_<constraint>, and at least one factor relativity equal the displayed values within cd_tolerance, and that the saved point honours the selected threshold (feasibility). This converts the only real-solver save path from shape-only to value-pinning and would fail on the #16 divergence.

findings.title: No test for the Utf8 apply-input column missing a canonicalised numeric ratebook level (#17 residual silent neutral-1.0 miss)
findings.description: Catalog #17 (medium, executed-repro) confirms a live silent-mispricing: a ratebook level saved as canonical '25' (from a Float64/Int64 banding-source) is silently missed at apply time when the OPTIMISER_APPLY INPUT column is Utf8 carrying literal '25.0', because _rating_key_expr leaves Utf8 values verbatim ('25.0' != '25'), the join misses, and onMissing='neutral' applies factor 1.0 (dropping the solved relativity, loud only in logs). The apply-agreement suite exhaustively covers the SAVE side and the apply side ONLY with Float64/Int frames, which DO canonicalise to '25' and match (test_float_frame_column_vs_string_levels:108, test_float64_levels_round_trip_solve_save_apply_with_zero_misses:479). The TestFloatEmittedLevelsCanonicalisedAtSave class docstring (459-477) declares '3b.10 FIXED' and asserts 'A Float64 factor column therefore round-trips solve->save->apply with every row matching its own solved level: zero misses' — but the residual #17 bug is precisely a Utf8 apply-input column (a distinct CSV/JSON source or upstream cast) against the canonical '25' level, which is never fed. The 'FIXED' framing risks giving false confidence that the apply-side dtype-divergence miss is covered when it is not.
findings.evidence: All apply frames in the suite are numeric: pl.DataFrame({'age':[25.0,...]}) (113, 499, 543), pl.DataFrame({'age':[25,26]}) (125). No test builds an apply frame with a Utf8/string '25.0' column and asserts the join either matches the saved '25' level or fails loudly. Catalog #17 repro: '[apply] Utf8 "25.0" input -> age_optimised_factor = 1.0 with a rating_table_lookup_misses warning'. Catalog #17 fix: 'Add a regression test pinning that a Float64-saved level is matched by a Utf8 "25.0" apply column (or rejected loudly), covering single-column and composite tables.'
findings.recommended_fix: Add a TDD test that solves/saves a Float64 banding-source factor (saved level '25'), then applies the artifact to a Utf8 apply-input column carrying '25.0', and asserts the intended behaviour (after fix: either the join matches and gives the solved factor, or it raises a loud config error) instead of the current silent neutral 1.0. Cover a composite table too. Until the bug is fixed, the test documents the silent miss as a failing test.

findings.title: No test for a finite fractional Float64 scenario_index being silently truncated on Int32 cast (#18), only the NaN case is covered
findings.description: Catalog #18 (medium, executed-repro) confirms a finite non-integer Float64 scenario_index (e.g. [2.0, 2.5]) PASSES the finiteness contract and is then silently truncated by .cast(pl.Int32) to [2, 2], collapsing two distinct scenario rows into one grid key and corrupting the optimised scenario set with no error. The existing validation tests give false confidence here: test_validate_and_project_rejects_non_finite_float_scenario_index (299) asserts a float scenario_index with NaN IS named/rejected, and test_validate_and_project_keeps_only_price_contour_columns (test_optimiser_contracts.py:473) asserts the projected scenario_index dtype is Int32 — but neither feeds a FINITE fractional float to exercise the integrality/truncation hole. The catalog explicitly notes the source IS finiteness-checked (so 2.5 passes); the gap is integrality, which is wholly untested. There is also a scenario_index ORDER test (test_optimiser_contracts.py:619, test_build_grid_rejects_interleaved_quote_blocks_loudly) but it uses clean Int32 values, so it does not cover float truncation either.
findings.evidence: test_validate_and_project_rejects_non_finite_float_scenario_index (308) uses pl.Series([0.0, float('nan')], dtype=pl.Float64) — only NaN, never a finite fractional like 2.5. Grep across tests/test_optimiser* for '2.5'/'floor'/'integral'/'truncat' returns no scenario_index integrality test. Catalog #18 fix: 'A regression test should feed Float64 scenario_index [2.0, 2.5] and assert a 400, plus assert integer scenario_index still passes.'
findings.recommended_fix: Add a TDD test that feeds _validate_and_project a Float64 scenario_index of [2.0, 2.5] for one quote and asserts a 400 contract error naming scenario_index (after the integrality guard is added), plus a positive test that an all-integral Float64 [0.0,1.0,2.0] and a native Int32 column still pass losslessly. This pins integrality, not just finiteness.

findings.title: _frontier_point_constraint_value tests omit the prefix-collision case (constraint named 'objective' reads total_objective)
findings.description: _frontier_point_constraint_value resolves a constraint by string-prefix fallback total_<name> -> constraints[<name>] -> bare <name> on a flat point dict. The catalog 'refuted' adjudication for this function confirmed the prefix-collision MECHANIC is real: _frontier_point_constraint_value({'total_objective':100.0,...}, 'objective') returns 100.0 — i.e. a constraint literally named 'objective' reads the objective TOTAL (via total_objective) rather than its own value; a constraint named to collide with total_/lambda_ prefixes maps to the wrong value. The two tests here only exercise the benign happy-path chain (total_volume wins, then constraints dict, then bare key) and the all-missing case. They never feed a colliding constraint name, so a regression that worsened or a fix that hardened the collision would be untested, and the wrong-value behaviour for a colliding name is silently blessed by omission. The finding was severity-calibrated down because a real-world constraint named 'objective' is unusual, but the unit is cheap to pin and the wrong-value path is genuinely reachable.
findings.evidence: Test only asserts {'total_volume':0.9,...},'volume' -> 0.9; {'constraints':{'volume':0.7},...},'volume' -> 0.7; {'volume':0.5},'volume' -> 0.5 (13402-13419). No assertion for name=='objective' against a dict containing total_objective. Catalog refuted-section entry: "_frontier_point_constraint_value({'total_objective':100.0,...}, 'objective') -> 100.0 (returns the OBJECTIVE total via the f\"total_{name}\" prefix)".
findings.recommended_fix: Add a test pinning the intended behaviour for a constraint whose name collides with a reserved prefix (e.g. 'objective'): either assert it resolves to the constraint's own value (if the function is hardened to disambiguate) or document/guard the collision loudly. This locks the resolver against silent wrong-value mapping.

findings.title: Non-convergence warning test is a conditional no-op when the solve converges
findings.description: The test runs a real solve with max_iter=1 intending to force non-convergence, then asserts the warning only inside `if not result['converged']:`. If the solve happens to converge in one iteration (trivial inputs, or any future solver/data drift), the guard is False and the test asserts nothing — it passes vacuously without ever verifying the non-convergence warning it exists to check. This is the classic conditional-assertion anti-pattern: the test cannot fail to catch a regression where the warning stops being emitted on genuine non-convergence, because it sidesteps the assertion whenever convergence occurs. It gives coverage credit for the warning path without guaranteeing the path is exercised.
findings.evidence: Lines 4885-4887: `result = status['result']` then `if not result['converged']: assert 'warning' in result`. No assertion that result['converged'] is actually False, so the meaningful assert is skipped on any converged run.
findings.recommended_fix: Make non-convergence deterministic and assert it unconditionally: construct inputs/config that provably cannot converge in the iteration budget, assert result['converged'] is False, then assert 'warning' in result (and ideally assert the warning text). Remove the `if` guard so a missing warning on real non-convergence fails the test.

findings.title: Test encodes the swallow-all-frontier-errors-while-completed contract (#43) as intended
findings.description: Catalog #43 (low) documents that _finalize_solve_result wraps the entire frontier sweep in `except Exception` and, on any failure, sets result['frontier_error'] while still transitioning the job to status='completed' with progress=1.0 and frontier=None — so a programmatic consumer keying on status would assume a frontier is present, and the catch is too broad (a real TypeError/KeyError programming bug is also swallowed). This test pins exactly that: a RuntimeError side_effect on solver.frontier yields status=='completed', frontier is None, frontier_error == 'Frontier unavailable: frontier exploded', and the /solve/status endpoint returns completed. The catalog explicitly flags this test as encoding the current contract that must be updated in lockstep if the catch is narrowed to specific frontier/solver exception types (so real programming errors propagate and fail the job). Listed as lower-value/lower-confidence because the behaviour is deliberate, documented, and the primary solve genuinely succeeded; it is included because it is a named 'test codifies current behaviour' that blocks the catalog's recommended narrowing.
findings.evidence: Lines 8161 mock_solver.frontier.side_effect = RuntimeError('frontier exploded'); 8175-8178 assert status=='completed', frontier is None, frontier_error=='Frontier unavailable: frontier exploded'. Catalog #43: 'an existing test (test_optimiser_routes.py:8140-8187) encodes the current contract and would need updating in lockstep.'
findings.recommended_fix: If #43 is actioned (narrow the catch to frontier/solver exception types and add a machine-readable frontier_status), update this test so a genuine programming-error exception propagates and fails the job, while a true solver/infeasibility error still surfaces as a non-fatal frontier_error on a completed job. Keep the non-fatal contract only for the expected exception family.
